Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verse 1:

"Hal ataka ... al-Ghashiyah" (88:1)

Through this opening, the surah turns hearts towards Allah and draws attention to the signs of Allah present in this universe. It tells that man will have to render an account on the Day of Resurrection and face reward and punishment, and that this is a certain matter. This is expressed with great emphasis through the interrogative form, which is emphatic or affirmative (istifhami ta'kidi ya taqriri). This interrogative style also indicates that before this surah, this matter has been repeatedly emphasized and reminded. Therefore, here the Resurrection is given a new name: al-Ghashiyah (the Overwhelming), meaning a calamity whose horrors will overwhelm people. This is a new name, but through this name attention is drawn to the terror of the Resurrection. Several names have come for the Resurrection in this regard: al-Tammah, al-Sakhkhah, al-Ghashiyah and al-Qari'ah, and all these names are appropriate to the themes of this part (of the Qur'an).

Regarding the question "Has there reached you the news of al-Ghashiyah?", the Messenger of Allah ﷺ understood that this question was being addressed to him first. Whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited or heard this surah, it seemed as though he had heard it for the first time and it was being revealed directly from Allah at that moment. Upon hearing this address from Allah, he would become alert and consider it to be Allah's address, and his feelings would be as if he had just received and heard it. Ibn Abi Hatim narrates from Ibn Muhammad al-Tanafisi, from Abu Bakr ibn Abbas, from Abu Ishaq, from Umar ibn Maymun that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by a woman who was reciting:

"Hal ataka ... al-Ghashiyah" (88:1), "Has there reached you the news of al-Ghashiyah?" Then he stood up and said, "Yes, the news has reached me."

Nevertheless, the address is to everyone who hears or recites the Qur'an, because the matter of al-Ghashiyah is the matter of the Qur'an, which repeatedly mentions the Resurrection. The Qur'an warns people by reminding them of the Resurrection and gives good tidings, and it stirs up motives of action and caution in fearful, sensitive and God-conscious hearts. Along with fear and caution, the Qur'an also teaches the waiting for hope and success, so that the human conscience does not die in heedlessness.

And after saying, "Has there reached you the news of the overwhelming calamity?", the headline of this news is given.

Here the scene of punishment is shown before the scene of blessings, because the question concerned the terrors of the Day of Judgment. It is told that people will be in a state of great fear, weary and worn out, and cowed by terror. They spent their whole lives in struggle, and became tired and defeated, yet their deeds turned out to be worthless, and no one accepted them. Their final end was also ruined, and they gained nothing but calamity and loss. Thus their fatigue, anxiety and helplessness only increased.

(3) "Labouring and toiling," [they will be] exhausted and worn out. In the world they will have been striving only for themselves and their children, toiling for the world and for its greed and avarice. Now the outcome lies before them: what was due to them in the world they received, but in the Hereafter there is nothing but darkness. Now they face the Hereafter in humiliation, distressed, losers, ruined and despairing. And along with this disgrace and abasement comes a painful punishment.

(4) "Burning in a fierce fire" [they will be]. They will taste it and endure its hardships.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verse 5:

Tusqa min 'aynin aniyah (88:5): "They will be given to drink from a boiling spring." Aniyah means extremely hot, boiling.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verses 6–7:

﴿They shall have no food except from a thorny plant, which neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger.﴾ 

Regarding the meaning of "ḍarī" (ضریع), there are two opinions. One is that it is a tree that will grow within Hell itself, just as the Qur'an mentions zaqqūm as a tree that grows at the bottom of Hell. The second opinion is that it is a thorny shrub that clings to the ground. When it is green it is called shibriq, and when it is cut and dried it is called ḍarī'. Camels graze on it. When it is dry, even camels cannot eat it, because its taste is bitter. In any case, whatever the meaning, this is the kind of food of which it is said, just as it is said about drink that they will drink ghassalīn or ghassāq, and whatever food is there will neither fatten them nor satisfy their hunger.

What will this punishment of the Hereafter be like? The truth is that in this world we cannot imagine it. Here its qualities are described so that we may be able to conceive of the worst punishment: disgrace, weakness, hopelessness, the burning of the hottest fire, zamharīr (that is, extreme cold), hot water of the most scalding kind to drink, and a food of such a kind that even camels could not eat it, and even if they did eat it, it would bring them no benefit. From these attributes, what settles in our feelings is an extreme degree of grief and anguish. But the punishment of the Hereafter is far more severe than our imaginings. And what it will be, only one who is afflicted with it can tell. We seek refuge in Allah! And on the other hand, the people of faith:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verses 8–9:

وجوہ یومئذ ........................................ مبثوثة

The faces of the people of Paradise will show on that Day that they are people who eat and drink. They will be deeply content because of the good pleasure of Allah. They will dwell among blessings. Their deeds will be looked upon with approval, they will be praised, and they will receive rewards. Besides this, they will attain an elevated spiritual awareness that Allah is pleased with their deeds, and they will see that Allah is pleased. No one can attain greater spiritual peace than this: that a person becomes content with good works, that their end is good, and then they see that their Lord is pleased with them and enter the Gardens. This is why the Qur'an mentions the good pleasure of Allah and spiritual joy before the material blessings of the Gardens, and after that the mention is made of their places within the Gardens.

Surah 88 (al-Ghashiyah), verse 10: "In a lofty garden."

(In a lofty Garden) They will be in an exalted paradise. They will be elevated in their own essence, elevated in honour, elevated in the ranks of their dwellings, and elevated in their stations. In short, a sense of loftiness will pervade their feelings.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verse 11:

"لا تسمع ... لاغية" (88:11): "They will not hear therein any idle talk." In this expression a whole atmosphere and a world of meanings has been packed. There will be rest, there will be tranquility, there will be peace and security, there will be love and contentment, there will be gatherings of friends, families and offspring will be united, there will be purity and cleanliness, and they will be far removed from every futile word. There will be no matter in which there is not well-being and safety for them. Such an atmosphere is itself a blessing; this condition is itself good fortune and felicity. When a person contemplates the difficulties and bitterness of worldly life, how much idle talk, quarrels, disputes, bickering, noise and clamour, censure and reproach, lies and deceit, and mischief and corruption exist here, and then contemplates the atmosphere of Paradise, which is tranquil, peaceful, full of love and fresh, and then this comprehensive expression of the Qur'an:

"لا تسمع ... لاغية" (88:11): "They will not hear therein any idle talk." These very words contain softness, ease and freshness. Their pronunciation is also melodious, soft and easy. From this it becomes known that the life of the believers in this world, and especially the life of the workers of the Islamic movement, is in fact a model of Paradise, as they keep away from idle and obscene talk and from wrangling and contention. This is, as it were, a preparation for the life of Paradise.

Thus, through the description of the conditions of Paradise, this bright and lofty meaning is presented, and after this there is mention of the blessings of Paradise which are a source of satisfaction for the human senses. These are mentioned in a form that man can imagine, but in Paradise these things will be in a form to which the souls of the people of Paradise will have progressed. And what will that form be? It will be known only to those who have experienced them.

Therein will be flowing springs. A flowing spring is one from which water is gushing forth; in flowing springs there is beauty, the movement of water, and the means of quenching thirst, all of which are beautiful. Flowing water is a manifestation of a kind of life, and it harmonizes with the human soul, which is flowing and dynamic. This scene and its inner beauty both reach down into the depths of human sensibility.
Fīhā ........................ marfū'a (88:13): "In it will be raised couches." The loftiness also points to both cleanliness and purity.

The Qur'anic quotation: ﴿وَأَكْوَابٌ مَّوْضُوعَةٌ﴾ (88:14).

"And cups placed [ready at hand]." This means they will be set out in rows, so that pure wine may be drunk from them, and the people of Paradise will have no need to ask for anything; everything will be prepared for them.

Surah 88 has 26 verses, and the Arabic here is actually 88:15, so I'll translate the passage as given.

And cushions arranged in rows (Qur'an 88:15). That is, cushions filled with soft material, which a person uses for comfort and enjoyment.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verse 16:

﴿وَزَرَابِيُّ مَبْثُوثَةٌ﴾ [88:16] "And fine carpets spread out all around." Carpets that are woolen, placed here and there for adornment and comfort.

These are the amenities whose like we see in this world, and the mention here of the amenities of Paradise in these terms is for our understanding. But what the amenities there will be like, and their reality, relates to their use there. Only those whose destiny is written for Paradise will be able to describe them.

It is futile to debate whether we should describe the nature and condition of the amenities of Paradise here, or the conditions of the punishment of the Hereafter. This is because the nature of things and their utility can be manifested in such a way that human perception of them becomes complete. The perceptive faculty of the people of the earth functions within the limited sphere of these earthly senses. When these people enter Paradise, all the limits and restrictions upon their perceptive faculty will be removed, and there their soul, feeling and perception will all advance greatly. Just as their perceptive faculty will advance there, so too the meanings of words will become broader there, and the state of their delight, longing, understanding and perception will be entirely different. Therefore, its reality cannot be recorded by us here.

Here we can only say that the mind will have the highest conception of pleasure, luxury, sweetness and delight, and we can say this only according to our own experience. The true reality will come into our knowledge only when Allah, glorified is His majesty, bestows upon us this honour there.

Here the journey of study into the world of the Hereafter ends, and we return to this outward universe that stands before us, within which the governance of the Almighty Lord is before our eyes, in which Allah's craftsmanship is distinguished, in which the things created by Allah appear distinguished. From them it becomes known that after this life there is a higher life, that beyond this earth there is a higher realm, and that death is not the end, but the outcome of people is something else.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verse 17:

"Will they not look at the camels, how they have been created? And at the sky, how it has been raised? And at the mountains, how they have been set up? And at the earth, how it has been spread out?" (88:17-20)

These are only four short verses, yet within them a complete picture of the environment of Arab society, the first audience of the Qur'an, has been drawn, and along with it a map of the whole universe: the sky, the earth, the mountains, and, upon the earth, the animal beauty of the camel. The camel is singled out because its creation is highly intricate and its importance for the Arabs is well established. Wherever a person may be, these scenes are before him: the sky, the mountains, the level earth, and upon it all kinds of living creatures. Whatever the stage of knowledge and understanding a person has reached, these scenes remain the focus of his knowledge, perception and interest. If a person reflects on the structure of these things, he can find in them the proofs and evidences that can guide him to the power behind this universe.

All these scenes have a miraculous quality. In them are manifest aspects of the Creator's craftsmanship for which there is no parallel in human discovery. These things are entirely sufficient for a person to form in his mind a basic, correct belief and a correct conception. This is why the Qur'an repeatedly points to them.

"Will they not look at the camels, how they have been created?" (88:17). For the first audience of the Qur'an, an Arab, the camel was important because he travelled on it, drank its milk, ate its meat, and made clothing and bedding from its hair and hide. It was, as it were, the great source of supply for his life and a major asset of his life. Moreover, the camel possessed certain features that distinguished it from other animals. One feature was that, despite its bulk, strength and massive body, it is such a gentle animal that even a small child who drives it is obeyed with great docility. Furthermore, the more benefits people derive from it, the easier it is to look after. Its food and grazing are easily available, and a person does not have to labour much to feed it. Of all domestic animals, it endures hunger, thirst, hardship and harsh conditions the most. Then, in the context in which God presents it here, its structure is most fitting. Its details are coming.

This is why the Qur'an told its audience: consider the creation of the camel; it is always before you. There is no need to go far away, and no great learning is required to reflect on it.

"Will they not look at the camels, how they have been created?" (88:17). They do not reflect on its structure and its creation. And then they do not reflect on how closely its structure harmonises with the purpose of its creation, and how well it fulfils that purpose. How well it discharges its duties in Arab society and in the Arab environment. Was the camel made by a human being? Did the camel come into being on its own? If neither of these is the case, then there must necessarily be a Creator. And since there is a Creator, He is most wise, for He created such a wondrous and beneficial creature.

"And do they not look at the sky, how it has been raised?" (88:18)

Throughout the Qur'an, people are invited again and again to look at the heavens with a contemplative gaze. The people of the desert should look at and reflect upon the sky even more, for the inhabitants of the desert have, at all times, a delightful taste and signs with the sky, as though the sky belongs to them. The sky is indeed spread above the deserts. The sky, with all its splendours, stands above the desert. Its bright and open days, the enchanting and beautiful time of midday and the unique time of sunset, in which a world of meanings lies hidden, the sky with its vast nights, its shining stars and beautiful stories, and then its beautiful and luminous scenes of dawn, are all present before you.

This sky, above the vastness of the deserts: do these people not look at it, how it has been raised up high? Without pillars, how are these heights sustained? Within it, billions upon billions of stars have been scattered, and within it have been placed such beauty, such grace, and such signs. Neither did humans raise it up, nor did it rise up on its own. Therefore there must be One who raised it up in this way, who brought it into existence. This kind of observation and this kind of reflection do not require vast or deep knowledge; they require only a discerning, insightful gaze.

Wa-ilal-jibali ... nusibat (88:19): "And do they not look at the mountains, how they have been raised up?" To an Arab, mountains were of great importance. It was among the mountains that the Arabs sought refuge in difficult times. In various stages, it was the mountains that served as their companions and friends. When a person looks upon mountain scenes, he receives deep psychological signals from them. In the system of the mountains there appears a grandeur; a beauty becomes visible. A person, considering himself lowly, takes shelter among them, finds peace at the foot of the mountains, and in this natural environment turns towards God; and in these lofty mountains a person thinks that he is closer to Allah. Thus at the foot of high mountains he rises somewhat above the clamour of the earth and its petty activities. This was neither a purposeless matter nor an accidental act: before prophethood, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would withdraw into the Cave of Hira on Mount Thawr. Therefore, those who seek everlasting elevation of spirit should let their souls, for a period, be far from worldly pollutions. The words here that come under consideration regarding the mountains are:

Kayfa nusibat (88:19): "That is, how they have been fixed upon the earth." These words are more in harmony with the atmosphere of the scene.

"And at the earth, how it has been spread out?" This spread-out earth is before our eyes. It has been made easy for living upon, for walking on it, and for working on it. Was it spread out by people? Clearly they did not spread it, for the earth existed before the creation of human beings. Do they not reflect upon this? Why does the question not arise in their minds: who is the One who spread it out? And who is the One who set it in such order that it becomes fit for life?

These scenes give important indications to the human heart. Through mere reflection and contemplation, a person receives these indications, and these indications are sufficient to awaken intuition and rouse the human conscience. Through these indications, a person turns his attention to his Originator, his Creator, and to the Creator of this entire universe.

In depicting this cosmic scene, the balance and harmony that have been observed deserve some attention, so that it becomes known in what beautiful language the Qur'an addresses human beings, and how greatly artistic excellences have been observed in it, and how these two things become woven into the sentiments of a conscious believer.

In this scene, the lofty sky and the spread-out earth have been shown. But the heights of the mountains are not horizontal, nor have they fallen upon the earth; rather, they are set firmly, set in such a way as the hump is upon a camel. In this scene there are two horizontal lines and two vertical lines, yet they are mutually proportionate, and this is the particular style of the Holy Qur'an according to which it presents scenes. The manner of expression is concise, but it is depictive.

The first journey was in the world of the Hereafter; the second was an observational journey through the scenes of this universe that were before us. Now the direction of address turns toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): he is directed to the limits of his duties and obligations, and it is told what the nature of his responsibilities is. In the same way, a final nudge is given to people's sentiments, so that hearts that are asleep may be awakened with regard to the Islamic call.

Therefore remind them. You are only a reminder. (Surah al-Ghashiyah 88:21)

Remind them of the events of the Hereafter, and also show them the signs in this universe. Your great duty is to remind. This is a defined and destined duty. In the matter of the Islamic call, your role is only to the extent that you convey the message. After that, you have neither the right to do anything more, nor is it your responsibility. Your duty is to convey the call; beyond that, you are not obliged to compel anyone to accept Islam.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verse 22:

"You are not one to compel them." Because the master of hearts is Allah. You cannot turn their hearts by force. The hearts are between the fingers of Allah. It is Allah's work that He turns whichever heart He wills toward faith.

Some people have the misunderstanding that if the duty of the Prophet ﷺ was only to convey the message, then why was jihad made obligatory? Jihad was not made obligatory so that people would be made believers, but so that the obstacles on the path of conveying the message would be removed. The aim was that the message of religion should not fail to reach people, and that no one who accepts Islam should be subjected to persecution. The purpose of jihad was that the political obstacles in the way of conveying the religion be removed. The essential duty of the Messenger is, in any case, the call to the religion.

These indications and instructions, that the duty of the Messenger of Allah is only to convey the message, are repeated again and again in the Quran, and there are several reasons for this. The first reason is that if people do not accept after the message has been conveyed, the Messenger of God should not be distressed; he should be assured that he has discharged his duty. He should be content and entrust the people to the decree of Allah, that He does whatever He wills. Because in the hearts of human beings, especially of those who carry out the work of the Islamic call, there is a strong desire that their mission succeed and prevail, and that everyone accept it. Therefore Allah repeatedly emphasized that the task of the caller is to call, and that he should work with such sincerity that he removes personal desire and personal preference from the account of the call. He should continue the work of calling, and leave the outcome to Allah. What it is to Him whether someone becomes a believer or a disbeliever? Especially in circumstances where conditions in a society are not favorable for the Islamic call, people are far from religion, and there are material and political obstacles in the way of religion, the caller should not be distressed.

The fact that the Islamic call is a pure good, and every human being desires that people enter into it, is shown by the intensity with which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is repeatedly addressed and reminded that his task is only to convey the message, and that he cannot compel anyone. Yet the Messenger of Allah was the Prophet of God; he knew well the limits and bounds of his duty, and was well acquainted and trained in the system and destiny of Allah. For this reason too, the Quran has stated this point again and again with emphasis. But even if the duty of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ends with conveying the message, the matter of those who deny does not end in any case, and those who reject are not let off, nor do they return safe and sound to their homes. Allah exists, and all affairs are presented before Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verses 23–24:

"But whoever turns away and disbelieves, Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment." This is because they will return only to Allah, and it is He who will surely call them to account. This is the final proclamation of this surah, and it is a decisive and conclusive proclamation.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 88, verses 23–24:

"But whoever turns away and disbelieves, Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment." This is because they will return only to Allah, and it is He who will surely call them to account. This is the final proclamation of this surah, and it is a decisive and conclusive proclamation.

Surah 88, verses 25–26:

"Verily, to Us is their return, and then upon Us is their reckoning" (88:25–26). Thus the role of the Messenger ﷺ in the Islamic call is also bounded by limits. And even after him, every caller (da'i) is charged only with conveying the call. The duty of every caller is to keep reminding, while the reckoning belongs to Allah. They cannot flee from Allah, nor can they escape His accountability.

However, the callers of truth should also keep in mind that they must remove the obstacles placed in the path of the Islamic call, so that the call can reach people freely. The removal of obstacles is fulfilled through the obligation of jihad, as is known from the study of the Qur'an and the Sirah of the Messenger ﷺ. Therefore, the Islamic doctrine of jihad should be understood without any deficiency or excess. Let it not be that obstacles exist in the way of Islam and jihad is not undertaken. Nor should it be that the paths of propagation are open and people are made Muslim by the force of the sword.
